title: Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF): The Future of Flexible Broadcast Infrastructure
dek: Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF) explained simply — what it is, how it works, and why it became a key topic at NAB Show 2026 for modern broadcast infrastructure.
card_summary: Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF) explained simply — what it is, how it works, and why it became a key topic at NAB Show 2026 for modern broadcast infrastructure.
meta_description: Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF) explained simply — what it is, how it works, and why it became a key topic at NAB Show 2026 for modern broadcast infrastructure.
body_html:
The broadcast industry is moving away from the era of "fixed boxes." Following the buzz at NAB Show 2026, one term is dominating the conversation: Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF).

But what exactly is DMF, and why is it becoming the reference model for modern media houses? This guide breaks it down from the basics through to practical deployment considerations.

1. What is DMF? (The end of the "black box")

Traditionally, broadcast facilities were built using specialised physical hardware. You had one box for vision mixing, one for graphics, and another for audio. If you wanted to do more, you had to buy more boxes.

Dynamic Media Facilities (DMF) flips this model. It is a software-defined approach where broadcast functions — such as switching, mixing, graphics, and monitoring — run as software applications on shared IT servers.

The shift: we are moving from "hardware-centric" (fixed) to "software-defined" (fluid). The image above captures this transition clearly — a rack of single-purpose vendor boxes on one side, and a pool of generic servers hosting multiple media applications on the other.

2. How do you deploy a DMF setup?

DMF does not care where the processing happens. It leverages standard IT infrastructure to run high-end media tasks. You can deploy it on:

  • On-premise servers — running in local data centres inside the broadcast facility.
  • Public cloud — running as virtual instances on hyperscale cloud platforms.
  • Hybrid environments — a mix of on-premise and cloud, depending on the workload.

Instead of physical cables and patch panels, software functions are connected digitally. This means an entire studio workflow can be reconfigured in minutes instead of weeks.

3. What does "dynamic" actually mean?

In a traditional setup, capacity is static. In a DMF-based facility, capacity is elastic.

  • Flexibility — reconfigure workflows on demand.
  • Scalability — pull more compute when needed.
  • Elasticity — spin up or shut down workflows without hardware changes.

4. A simple comparison: the "pizza oven" vs. the "cloud kitchen"

Traditional facilities are like a single-purpose pizza oven — efficient at one thing, but built around a fixed output.

DMF is more like a modern cloud kitchen — the same underlying infrastructure can prepare different outputs on demand, scale up when orders spike, and scale down when they quieten. The kitchen adapts to demand instead of forcing demand to fit the kitchen.

5. Real-world use cases

  • Live sports and events — spin up additional channels or feeds during peak events, then release the capacity afterwards.
  • Pop-up channels — launch a temporary channel for a tournament, election, or seasonal programming without deploying new hardware.
  • Remote production (REMI) — distribute production roles across locations, with the processing layer running centrally on shared infrastructure.

6. DMF vs. traditional facilities

Dimension Traditional Facility Dynamic Media Facility (DMF)
Hardware Dedicated single-purpose boxes Shared IT servers
Scaling Fixed ports Elastic software instances
Setup time Weeks Minutes
Skillset Broadcast engineering Broadcast IT, networking, DevOps

7. Challenges to consider

DMF is not a drop-in upgrade. The shift introduces real operational changes that broadcast teams need to plan for:

  • IT skill requirements — teams need comfort with virtualisation, containers, and cloud-native operations alongside traditional broadcast knowledge.
  • Software and network-based troubleshooting — the failure modes move from "replace the bad box" to "inspect the logs, check the network, trace the container."
  • Cultural shift — moving from a hardware-first mindset to a platform-first one takes time, and it is as much about process and training as it is about technology.

Bottom line

DMF is not about replacing everything overnight. It is about building flexibility into broadcast infrastructure so that systems can evolve instead of being replaced. For facilities planning their next refresh cycle, the question is no longer "which box do we buy?" — it is "which workloads do we run on shared infrastructure, and which still need a dedicated appliance?"

That is the conversation NAB 2026 brought to the front of the room, and it is the conversation that will shape broadcast capex and opex decisions for the rest of the decade.

title: Avid and Google Cloud Partner to Deliver Agentic AI to Media Production
dek: Avid integrates Google Gemini and Vertex AI into Media Composer and Content Core for natural-language media search and autonomous post-production task management.
card_summary: Avid integrates Google Gemini and Vertex AI into Media Composer and Content Core for natural-language media search and autonomous post-production task management.
meta_description: Avid integrates Google Gemini and Vertex AI into Media Composer and Content Core for natural-language media search and autonomous post-production task management.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Avid and Google Cloud have announced a multi-year strategic partnership to embed Google's Gemini models and Vertex AI directly into two core Avid platforms: Media Composer and the new cloud-native Avid Content Core. The stated goal is to shift video editing from a largely manual process into an AI-assisted workflow, specifically targeting the time-intensive task of media discovery across large production libraries. The partnership will be demonstrated live at NAB Show 2026 (April 18-22) at both company booths.

Technical Deep Dive

The integration targets two distinct layers of Avid's technology stack. In Media Composer, the industry-standard NLE for professional film and television, Gemini's multimodal capabilities are being used to enable natural-language search across media bins. Rather than manually logging clips with keywords, editors can describe what they need, referencing visual actions, dialogue fragments, or emotional tone, and the system surfaces matching content from the project timeline or connected storage.

The second integration point is Avid Content Core, a cloud-native asset management platform positioned as the successor to Avid's on-premises MediaCentral/Interplay architecture. Content Core on Google Cloud adds Vertex AI for automated metadata generation, content classification, and what Avid describes as agentic workflows. These are AI assistants that can autonomously handle multi-step production tasks such as matching visual styles across sequences, identifying emotional cues in raw footage, and streamlining metadata logging without constant human direction.

What the announcement does not specify: latency benchmarks for real-time search during active editing sessions, the cost model for Vertex AI inference at scale, whether the Gemini integration requires Content Core or works with existing Nexis and MediaCentral environments, and how the system handles rights-managed or restricted content in multi-tenant cloud deployments.

Deployment Roadmap

For broadcast engineering teams evaluating this partnership, the critical question is infrastructure dependency. Content Core is cloud-native and runs on Google Cloud. Facilities with existing on-premises Nexis storage and MediaCentral deployments will need to determine whether the AI features require a full migration to Content Core or if Gemini integration extends to hybrid architectures.

Teams considering early adoption should plan for: a Google Cloud account with Vertex AI access, evaluation of data residency requirements (particularly for European broadcasters under GDPR), bandwidth assessment for cloud-based media search against production-scale libraries, and a parallel testing period running AI-assisted and traditional workflows side by side before committing editorial operations.

Operational Wins

The immediate value proposition is speed-to-edit. In large-scale productions, the time spent searching for specific footage is a measurable operational cost. If Gemini's natural-language search meaningfully reduces that time, the ROI case writes itself. The deeper strategic play is Content Core's positioning as a cloud-native replacement for on-premises MAM, a transition that, if executed well, eliminates hardware refresh cycles and scales storage elastically. The risk: cloud egress costs and latency for facilities that have not built out their WAN infrastructure for high-bandwidth media operations.

title: Blackmagic Design Launches DaVinci Resolve 21 at NAB 2026
dek: DaVinci Resolve 21 launches alongside new hardware at NAB 2026, continuing Blackmagic's approach of making professional colour, editing, VFX, and audio accessible.
card_summary: DaVinci Resolve 21 launches alongside new hardware at NAB 2026, continuing Blackmagic's approach of making professional colour, editing, VFX, and audio accessible.
meta_description: DaVinci Resolve 21 launches alongside new hardware at NAB 2026, continuing Blackmagic's approach of making professional colour, editing, VFX, and audio accessible.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Blackmagic Design has announced DaVinci Resolve 21 alongside multiple new hardware products at NAB 2026 (Booth N2502). CEO Grant Petty's product announcement continues the company's tradition of bundling major software and hardware releases into a single pre-show event. For post-production teams evaluating NLE ecosystems, this release cycle reinforces Blackmagic's position as the industry's primary alternative to subscription-based editing platforms.

Technical Deep Dive

DaVinci Resolve has evolved from a dedicated colour grading tool into a comprehensive post-production platform integrating editing, visual effects and motion graphics (Fusion), colour grading, audio post-production (Fairlight), and delivery within a single application. The hardware announcements historically include new camera models, video I/O devices, switchers, and monitoring equipment designed to integrate tightly with Resolve's software ecosystem.

Blackmagic's hardware strategy provides the processing power (editing controllers, Decklink I/O cards, UltraStudio capture devices) that makes Resolve's professional features accessible on standard workstation hardware rather than requiring dedicated turnkey systems. This combined hardware-software approach lowers the barrier to entry for facilities that want professional-grade tools without the capital expenditure of traditional post-production hardware vendors.

Deployment Roadmap

Facilities using Avid Media Composer as their primary NLE may find Resolve 21 most valuable as a colour grading and finishing tool, accepting AAF/EDL/XML roundtrips from Avid for grade, then rendering back. Facilities looking to reduce per-seat licensing costs may evaluate Resolve as a primary NLE, though this requires assessing collaborative editing maturity relative to Avid's MediaCentral model.

Operational Wins

The persistent value proposition is economic: the free tier provides genuinely professional-grade tools at zero cost per seat. The Studio version (one-time purchase, no subscription) adds GPU-accelerated AI features, multi-user collaboration, and advanced HDR tools. For broadcast teams under budget pressure, the software cost of standing up a new edit suite is effectively zero. The capital expenditure shifts entirely to hardware, storage, and I/O.

title: Haivision Falkon X4: Four-Modem 5G Contribution for Live Sports and News
dek: Haivision's Falkon X4 brings four independent cellular modems with eight antennas to mobile video contribution, targeting live sports and 24/7 news.
card_summary: Haivision's Falkon X4 brings four independent cellular modems with eight antennas to mobile video contribution, targeting live sports and 24/7 news.
meta_description: Haivision's Falkon X4 brings four independent cellular modems with eight antennas to mobile video contribution, targeting live sports and 24/7 news.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Haivision has launched the Falkon X4, the newest addition to its Falkon family of 5G mobile video transmitters. The headline engineering specification: four independent cellular modems, each with 2x2 MIMO, providing eight total cellular antennas. This architecture targets the reliability problem that plagues mobile contribution in crowded venues. For live sports production and 24/7 news operations, this redundancy addresses a real operational risk that existing two-modem solutions cannot fully mitigate.

Technical Deep Dive

The Falkon X4 supports video up to 4K/UHD with 4:2:2 chroma subsampling, 10-bit colour depth, and HDR (PQ and HLG). The camera-mountable form factor supports both V-Mount and Gold Mount battery systems. Production capabilities include local recording, file forwarding, audio intercom, video return feed, and a data bridge for ancillary data transport.

For remote production workflows, the Falkon X4 offers remote camera control including camera shading, PTZ adjustment, and embedded timestamps for frame-accurate synchronisation across multiple transmitters. This is critical for multi-camera remote productions where all feeds must arrive in precise temporal alignment at a distant production switcher.

Deployment Roadmap

The primary deployment scenario is live sports remote production from stadiums and outdoor events where dedicated fibre is impractical. The four-modem architecture means engineering teams can provision SIMs from multiple carriers per event, hedging against congestion. For 24/7 news, Falkon X4 serves as the primary field contribution device, replacing satellite uplink trucks for routine live shots.

Operational Wins

The case is straightforward: fewer failed live shots. The four-modem architecture provides four independent cellular paths. If any single path degrades, the remaining three maintain the feed. The camera-mount form factor and battery compatibility mean no additional crew or equipment beyond the camera operator. For facilities already using Falkon X2, the X4 is a drop-in upgrade that doubles cellular redundancy without changing the production workflow.

title: Haivision Makito ONE: Multi-Codec Encoding and Decoding on a Single Blade
dek: Haivision's new Makito ONE combines dual-channel 4K encoding and decoding with H.264, HEVC, and JPEG XS support on a single hot-swappable blade.
card_summary: Haivision's new Makito ONE combines dual-channel 4K encoding and decoding with H.264, HEVC, and JPEG XS support on a single hot-swappable blade.
meta_description: Haivision's new Makito ONE combines dual-channel 4K encoding and decoding with H.264, HEVC, and JPEG XS support on a single hot-swappable blade.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Haivision is launching the Makito ONE at NAB 2026, a single-blade platform that combines dual-channel video encoding and decoding in one hot-swappable unit. The headline specification: support for H.264, HEVC, and JPEG XS codecs with both 3G-SDI and SMPTE ST 2110 connectivity. For facilities managing a mix of legacy SDI infrastructure and IP-native workflows, this consolidation into one blade reduces rack space and operational complexity in the contribution chain.

Technical Deep Dive

Makito ONE's architecture centres on multi-codec flexibility within a single hardware unit. The platform supports encoding and decoding of H.264 (AVC), HEVC (H.265), and JPEG XS, the visually lossless, ultra-low-latency codec gaining traction in ST 2110 production environments. Each blade handles up to dual 4K/UHD or quad 1080p HD channels simultaneously.

Connectivity options include 3G-SDI for legacy baseband integration and SMPTE ST 2110 with NMOS IS-04/IS-05 discovery and registration for IP-native deployments. This dual-interface approach means a single Makito ONE blade can sit at the boundary between an SDI router and an IP fabric, handling format conversion without separate gateway hardware. The platform scales from a single compact blade to 1RU and 4RU modular chassis supporting up to 18 hot-swappable blades, providing up to 36 HD/4K channels in a single chassis.

What Haivision has not disclosed: per-blade pricing, power consumption at full density, JPEG XS profile support details, and whether the NMOS implementation supports IS-07 and IS-08 in addition to baseline IS-04/IS-05.

Deployment Roadmap

The primary deployment scenario is contribution infrastructure consolidation. Facilities currently running separate encoder and decoder hardware from different vendors can evaluate Makito ONE as a single-platform replacement. The hot-swap chassis design makes this practical for mission-critical environments: a failed blade can be replaced without powering down the chassis or interrupting adjacent channels.

Operational Wins

Rack space reduction is the immediate win. For remote production operations, the multi-codec support means one hardware platform can handle both HEVC contribution links and JPEG XS studio-quality feeds within the same workflow, adapting codec selection to available bandwidth rather than requiring dedicated hardware per codec. The SRT protocol support ensures reliable transport over public internet, 4G, and 5G for mobile contribution and disaster-recovery failover paths.

title: NAB 2026 Preview: What Broadcast Engineers Should Be Watching This Week
dek: NAB Show 2026 opens this week. From Avid's agentic AI partnership with Google Cloud to Haivision's multi-codec Makito ONE, here are the technology trends for broadcast engineers.
card_summary: NAB Show 2026 opens this week. From Avid's agentic AI partnership with Google Cloud to Haivision's multi-codec Makito ONE, here are the technology trends for broadcast engineers.
meta_description: NAB Show 2026 opens this week. From Avid's agentic AI partnership with Google Cloud to Haivision's multi-codec Makito ONE, here are the technology trends for broadcast engineers.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

NAB Show 2026 opens at the Las Vegas Convention Center on April 18-22, and the pre-show announcements are already signalling where vendor investment and engineering attention are converging. Three themes dominate: agentic AI entering post-production workflows, multi-codec encoding platforms that bridge SDI and ST 2110 in a single blade, and 5G mobile contribution moving from demonstration to production deployment. For broadcast engineering teams, the question at this NAB is no longer whether these technologies work. It is whether they integrate cleanly into existing operational architectures without requiring a full infrastructure refresh.

Technical Deep Dive

The Avid-Google Cloud partnership, announced April 16, is the most architecturally significant announcement heading into the show. Embedding Gemini models and Vertex AI into Media Composer and the new cloud-native Content Core platform targets a real operational pain point: media discovery in large-scale productions. Natural-language search across media bins, automated metadata generation, and agentic workflows represent a meaningful step beyond the auto-tagging features that MAM vendors have been shipping since 2023.

On the contribution side, Haivision's Makito ONE consolidates encoding and decoding with H.264, HEVC, and JPEG XS plus SDI and ST 2110 connectivity on a single hot-swappable blade. Haivision's Falkon X4 mobile transmitter pushes 5G contribution further with a four-modem architecture providing eight cellular antennas for high-throughput stability in congested RF environments. Blackmagic Design's DaVinci Resolve 21 continues the company's strategy of bundling professional colour grading, editing, VFX, and audio tools into a single application at zero per-seat licensing cost. Grass Valley is expanding its LDX camera portfolio with the LDX 110 for triple-speed HD capture and demonstrating its Media Universe ecosystem.

Deployment Roadmap

For engineering teams heading to NAB this week, the practical evaluation agenda should prioritise three areas. First, cloud dependency: the Avid-Google Cloud announcement raises questions about data residency, egress costs, and hybrid architecture support. Second, codec consolidation: the Makito ONE's multi-codec approach is only valuable if it supports the specific profiles and interface standards your facility requires. Third, 5G contribution: if your operation relies on mobile video for news gathering or sports, the Falkon X4's four-modem architecture deserves hands-on evaluation.

Operational Wins

The broader trend emerging from pre-NAB announcements is convergence: convergence of encode and decode functions, convergence of SDI and IP connectivity, convergence of manual editing and AI-assisted workflows, and convergence of on-premises and cloud infrastructure. For engineering teams, convergence means fewer boxes in the rack, fewer management interfaces to maintain, and fewer vendor-specific integration headaches. The risk is vendor lock-in, and the vendors making the strongest convergence arguments are the ones engineering teams should interrogate most carefully about open standards, API access, and exit paths.

title: Bitcentral Highlights Connected Media Workflows, Hybrid Infrastructure, and Automation at NAB Show 2026
dek: Bitcentral will showcase connected media workflows, hybrid storage strategies, metadata intelligence, and automation tools at NAB Show 2026, focusing on flexible newsroom, production, and linear channel operations.
card_summary: Bitcentral will showcase connected media workflows, hybrid storage strategies, metadata intelligence, and automation tools at NAB Show 2026, focusing on flexible newsroom, production, and linear channel operations.
meta_description: Bitcentral will showcase connected media workflows, hybrid storage strategies, metadata intelligence, and automation tools at NAB Show 2026, focusing on flexible newsroom, production, and linear channel operations.
body_html:
Source Attribution This article is based on the Bitcentral press release dated April 10, 2026, announcing the company's planned exhibits at NAB Show 2026, Booth W2823.
Independent technical interpretation by The Streamic.

Bitcentral is preparing to demonstrate a set of connected media workflow capabilities at NAB Show 2026, focusing on how broadcasters can modernize production, metadata handling, and linear operations without disrupting existing systems. The company will exhibit at Booth W2823.

The showcase emphasizes incremental modernization — introducing new capabilities alongside established systems rather than replacing them outright — an approach that reflects how most broadcasters actually upgrade their facilities in practice.

Workflow Interoperability Through Fusion Gateway

A central part of Bitcentral's showcase is Fusion Gateway, a cloud-based integration framework designed to link content, metadata, and operational workflows across third-party platforms. The framework uses scalable APIs to support new integrations while keeping existing production environments stable.

For engineering teams, this enables a more modular workflow design, where systems can be connected or extended without re-architecting the entire chain. In practice, this reduces the cost and risk associated with adding new tools — integrations become additive rather than disruptive.

Hybrid Infrastructure for Evolving Storage and Access Needs

Bitcentral will also highlight Fusion Hybrid Storage, which supports hybrid infrastructure strategies. This allows organizations to distribute storage across on-premises and cloud environments based on performance, cost, or accessibility requirements.

In practical terms, this gives operations teams more flexibility in how they manage media assets across different stages of the content lifecycle — keeping active production assets close to the edit suite while moving lower-tier content to more cost-effective cloud tiers.

Metadata Intelligence and Operational Automation

Metadata continues to play a growing role in production efficiency. Fusion Insights is positioned as a way to convert metadata into actionable intelligence, helping teams improve content discovery and make faster editorial decisions.

Automation also extends into linear operations through Central Control, which integrates traffic, assets, scheduling, and monitoring into a unified operational layer. This supports more reliable channel management and reduces manual intervention in day-to-day playout workflows.

Newsroom Workflow Efficiency

For newsroom environments, Core News provides tools for planning, scripting, editing, and multi-platform publishing. The focus is on reducing friction across the editorial workflow and enabling teams to move content through production pipelines more efficiently.

Industry Context

Broadcasters continue to adopt cloud, automation, and metadata-driven workflows, but many still rely on established systems that cannot be replaced overnight. Bitcentral's approach emphasizes incremental modernization, allowing organizations to introduce new capabilities while maintaining control over how their environments evolve.

For CTOs and operations leaders, the practical value of this kind of integration-first strategy is that it lets teams evaluate and adopt new capabilities at their own pace, without forcing a wholesale replatforming of systems that are already running reliably on air.
